title: Memory Safety and Error-Handling Patterns for Multi-language Services
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview:

This document defines the memory-safety, resource-management, and error-handling patterns that services at Redwood Inference should follow across Go, Rust, and Python codebases. The goal is consistent operational behavior, predictable failure modes, and CI/production guardrails that prevent classes of bugs that cause OOMs, silent data corruption, or noisy retries.

Scope and audience:
- Services (stateless and stateful) implemented in Go, Rust, or Python.
- Library code and shared SDKs consumed by multiple services.
- Engineers responsible for PR review, CI configuration, and runtime incident mitigation.

Principles (why these rules exist):
1. Fail fast and loudly: prefer deterministic, explicit failures over silent degradation.
2. Small, composable invariants: use clear ownership models so memory/resource lifetimes are obvious at call boundaries.
3. Observable failure modes: all recoverable and non-recoverable errors must be traceable with logs/metrics and correlate to SLO impact.
4. Language-appropriate idioms: enforce safety without forcing every language into the same mental model.

Patterns and rules (by language):

A. Go (services and SDKs)
- Ownership model: prefer value semantics for small structs; use pointers when sharing or mutating large buffers. Document ownership in function comments.
- Error propagation: return typed errors (wrapped via fmt.Errorf("%w") or errors.Join) and define sentinel errors only for cross-package contracts. Map to HTTP/GRPC status codes in a single location (service/error-mapper.go).
- Memory usage: avoid large in-memory buffers. Use io.Reader/io.Writer streaming for model artifacts and payloads > 4MB.
- Concurrency: use context.Context for cancellation. All goroutines spawned in request handling must be bound by ctx and joined or leak detectors enabled in tests.
- Linting/formatting: golangci-lint with the following minimum enables: govet, staticcheck, ineffassign, gocyclo (max 18). Commit hook requires go vet pass. Example snippet (CI):

  # .golangci.yml
  run:
    timeout: 5m
  linters:
    enable: [govet,staticcheck,errcheck,ineffassign,gocyclo]

- CI gates: go test -race, golangci-lint run, benchmark smoke test (alloc/op check).

B. Rust (components and low-level runtime)
- Ownership model: default to Rust ownership and borrowing. Use Arc<Mutex<T>> sparingly; prefer lock-free designs or explicit sharding when possible.
- Unsafe code: all unsafe blocks must be limited to isolated modules and accompany a short justification and safety comment referencing an ADR or RFC. Unsafe code requires two reviewers with at least one senior runtime engineer.
- Error handling: prefer Result<T, E> with small, typed error enums. Use thiserror or anyhow consistently in libraries vs binary crates (libraries: thiserror; binaries: anyhow with explicit mapping at boundary).
- Memory profiles: include nightly heap-snapshot CI job for runtime crates that manage model KV caches or long-lived buffers. Alert if resident set growth > 20% against baseline.
- Formatting: rustfmt with the standard toolchain; clippy in deny mode for pedantic lints on runtime-critical crates.

C. Python (orchestration and lightweight services)
- Ownership model: lean on immutable objects where possible for message passing. Avoid global mutable caches; prefer cache backends (redis/memcached) for cross-process caching.
- Type safety: use mypy with strict optional checks on public modules (mypy --strict).
- Error handling: explicit exception classes for domain errors. Catch broad exceptions only at top-level request handlers and re-raise structured errors for telemetry.
- Memory usage: prefer generators/iterators for streaming data; limit large in-process caches to configurable caps with eviction policies.

Cross-language conventions:
- Error contract and mapping: every service must map internal errors to a small set of service-level classifications: transient, permanent, rate-limited, auth-failure, resource-exhausted. Maintain an error-catalog.md in the repo root for any public API.
- Observability hooks: when returning or converting an error, include an error code and structured context fields that can be read by logging/tracing libraries. Example: {"code":"RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED", "model":"gpt-xl", "alloc_mb":2048}.
- CI and pre-merge gates:
  1. Static analysis (language-specific linters)
  2. Unit tests with coverage thresholds (>= 70% for new modules)
  3. Memory smoke test for changes touching buffers or caching (baseline comparison)
  4. Canary rollout playbook included in PR template for infra-impacting changes

Runtime guardrails and SLOs for memory-related regressions:
- Memory regression alert: if baseline RSS increases by > 20% or absolute delta > 512MB for a service lane, fail canary and open a memory-regression incident.
- Leak detector: use periodic heap-snapshot and allocation-rate metrics. SLO: allocation-rate increase (requests/sec normalized) must not exceed 10% over typical nightly baseline for safe releases.

Operational procedures (on-call and runbook snippets):
1. Symptom: service OOMs on model load.
   - Immediate: throttle autoscaler to zero new requests to affected zone; scale read-only fallback; trigger canary rollback.
   - Investigation: collect pprof/heap profiles (Go: pprof; Rust: heaptrack/Valgrind locally; Python: tracemalloc), annotate trace IDs and sample requests.
   - Mitigation: disable new model variants, pin to previous model binary, or increase node swap with caution.

2. Symptom: gradual RSS growth across replicas.
   - Immediate: trigger deployment with reduced concurrency and increased restart policy.
   - Investigation: run nightly heap diff and identify allocation hotspots, search for large retained objects tied to request IDs.

Review, PR expectations, and ownership:
- PR checklist (required before merge):
  - Tests added/updated (unit + memory smoke)
  - Linter and formatter CI green
  - Updated API error-catalog if error classifications changed
  - Reviewer from runtime team for changes touching memory or concurrency
- Ownership: module-level OWNERS file must list at least two reviewers. Unsafe or native bindings require an owner from eng-serving-runtime.

Examples and anti-patterns:
- Anti-pattern: catching Exception (Python) or panicking (Go) at deep call sites — hides root cause and breaks observability.
- Example: correct Go pattern for streaming large payloads:

  func StreamModelOutput(ctx context.Context, r io.Reader, w io.Writer) error {
    buf := make([]byte, 32*1024)
    for {
      n, err := r.Read(buf)
      if n > 0 {
        if _, wErr := w.Write(buf[:n]); wErr != nil {
          return fmt.Errorf("write-failure: %w", wErr)
        }
      }
      if err == io.EOF {
        return nil
      }
      if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read-failure: %w", err)
      }
    }
  }

- Example: Rust unsafe justification header (required):

  // SAFETY: We call C library X that returns a stable pointer for the lifetime of the allocator.
  // We pin T here to ensure no reallocation across the FFI boundary. See ADR-2025-ffi-pinning.
  unsafe fn from_ffi(ptr: *mut Raw) -> Box<T> { ... }

Enforcement and evolution:
- The standards in this document will be enforced via CI templates and periodic repo audits. Exceptions must be requested via a short RFC and approved by the runtime guild.
- This doc will be reviewed quarterly by the runtime and platform teams; backward-incompatible changes must be accompanied by a migration playbook.

References and related reading:
- Runtime memory model (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture
- ADR: FFI and unsafe patterns in runtime crates (link to ADRs folder)
- API error classification guidelines: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/error-classifications-2025

Appendix: CI checklist (copyable)
- run: go test ./... -race
- run: golangci-lint run --config .golangci.yml
- run: cargo test --all --release && cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
- run: python -m pytest && mypy --strict
